items.title: From Swiggy To Sweety: A Diwali Campaign Built On Curiosity - BW Marketing World
items.raw_summary: What happens when a brand that has spent years building recognition around its name decides to temporarily give it up? Ahead of Diwali, Swiggy appears to have done exactly that. The food delivery platform has given itself a new identity, calling itself ‘Sweety’, and in doing so, has turned an otherwise familiar brand touchpoint into an advertising property.Swiggy's Instagram display name has changed to ‘Sweety’. Its bio carries the line, “Sweets you 🧡 on time”, bringing the brand's familiar promise of timely delivery into a festive context. What initially appeared to be an unusual social media makeover has since extended into print advertising, employee communication and other brand-associated social media handles.Power Of An Integrated Brand EcosystemA print advertisement carries the message, ‘Oh Sweety, ghar aana’, alongside the line ‘Sweets you 🧡 on time.’ The visual features an orange delivery bag bearing the Sweety identity, with a modified version of the familiar Swiggy logo. The message is eye catching because it draws on the cultural familiarity of returning home during Diwali, while simultaneously making a reference to the brand's core delivery proposition.The campaign has also been extended through Swiggy's wider social media ecosystem. Swiggy Instamart has introduced itself as ‘Haan, woh main Sweety's chhota sibling’, while the delivery partner account carries the line ‘Sweety hone ka ghamand hai’.The participation has moved beyond brand-owned accounts, too. Mayur Hola, Swiggy's Head of Brand, shared his supposed new role as ‘Head of Halwai for Sweety’ on LinkedIn, signing off with the hashtag ‘#sameshitnewmithai’. Other employees have participated in similar communication, giving the exercise a more distributed, participatory character.This is where the campaign demonstrates an understanding of platform behaviour. Instagram allows the brand to experiment with its public-facing personality, while LinkedIn offers an opportunity to extend the joke through employees and leadership. Print, meanwhile, brings the idea into a traditional media environment, giving the campaign visibility beyond social media.The different executions also create multiple opportunities for consumers to encounter the same idea. Someone might notice the changed Instagram name, come across an employee's LinkedIn post and subsequently see the print advertisement. Each interaction adds another layer to the campaign.Swiggy is doing more than changing its name for Diwali; it is creating a festive persona around an established brand. What makes the campaign engaging is how it turns the brand's own identity into the central creative idea, using humour and curiosity to spark conversation.Turning Brand Identity Into An Advertising AssetWhile festive advertising’s traditional route relies on films centred on family, gifting and togetherness, Swiggy has taken a different path, making its own brand identity the centrepiece of the campaign.By replacing its familiar name with ‘Sweety’, Swiggy disrupted an established digital identity to capture attention. Its existing brand equity, from the orange colour to its recognisable visual language, ensures that the change sparks curiosity without losing brand recognition. This makes the name switch an effective attention-led marketing intervention.The distinction is important. A lesser-known brand attempting the same exercise might struggle to generate curiosity because it would first need to establish recognition. Swiggy, on the other hand, has the advantage of an established identity. It can temporarily play with that identity because consumers already know what lies behind it.The name ‘Sweety’ also works on more than one level. It sounds conversational, familiar and affectionate, while immediately establishing an association with sweets and mithai. Ahead of Diwali, when mithai becomes an integral part of household purchases, gifting and social exchanges, the word carries immediate cultural relevance.There is also a linguistic advantage. ‘Haan, woh main Sweety, now what to do?’ borrows from the casual, self-aware language of internet conversations. It does not sound like a conventional corporate announcement. Instead, it feels like a brand participating in a joke that consumers are expected to understand. That informality is central to the execution.The Curiosity EconomyAn important part of the Sweety exercise is that it leaves room for consumers to speculate.Why has Swiggy become Sweety? Is it launching a festive sweets collection? Is there a larger Diwali announcement? Is the name change itself the campaign?The lack of an immediate, elaborate explanation gives audiences an opportunity to participate in interpreting the activity.This is a form of curiosity-led communication. Rather than presenting the entire message upfront, the brand introduces an unexpected change and allows the audience to connect the dots.There is a difference between creating curiosity and creating confusion, though. Curiosity works when the audience has enough contextual clues to form a plausible connection. In this instance, the references to sweets, mithai, Diwali and timely delivery provide those clues.The name change is also relatively easy to understand across audience segments. It does not depend on a particularly niche meme or a complicated cultural reference. The humour is accessible, while the association with sweets is immediate.That gives the intervention a wider potential audience than a campaign built exclusively around an internet subculture.But participation cannot be assumed simply because a brand has changed its name. The real test is whether consumers begin using the name themselves, sharing the campaign, tagging the brand or bringing it into conversations that extend beyond its own social media pages.The difference between people noticing a brand and people actively participating in its communication is where the value of social-led campaigns becomes visible.The Final VerdictAs a teaser, Sweety is smart, well-layered and very Swiggy. The idea is simple enough to explain in one line, and the execution stretches across print, Instagram, sub-brands, delivery partners and LinkedIn in a way that feels coordinated, not cobbled together. The real test is the next move. A brand can change its name for a week, but it can only change what people do by giving them a reason to open the app.This is also where the campaign differs from a conventional rebranding exercise. The objective is not to change what Swiggy stands for, but to make the brand feel more culturally present during a specific consumption occasion.If the name change leads consumers towards a stronger association with festive sweets, timely delivery and the convenience of celebrating Diwali through Swiggy, the campaign will have achieved more than a social media moment. It demonstrates how a brand can turn a familiar identity into an unexpected advertising idea, and how sometimes the most effective way to get people talking about a brand is to give them a reason to ask what happened to its name.In today's day and time,, Swiggy has turned an Instagram display name into one of the more memorable Diwali campaigns of the year.
